paragraphs: The full moon hung low over Blackwood Manor, casting eerie shadows along its ivy-covered walls. Renowned detective Claire Harlow stepped out of her car, the gravel crunching beneath her feet, and surveyed the imposing mansion. Inside, four individuals awaited her arrival. Evelyn Blackwood, the wealthy and eccentric matriarch of the family, had been found dead in her study—poisoned, according to preliminary reports. Gathered in the house were Victor Blackwood, her brooding nephew with a history of financial troubles; Margaret Holloway, her lifelong assistant and confidante; Andrew Blackwood, her charming yet impulsive grandson; and Dr. Theodore Lang, the family physician with secrets of his own. Claire smoothed the lapel of her trench coat and stepped into the house, ready to unravel the truth buried beneath layers of deceit.

The heavy oak doors groaned open, and Claire was immediately met with tension thick enough to cut with a knife. In the grand foyer, the four suspects stood apart, each wearing a mask of controlled emotions. Victor paced back and forth like a caged animal, his dark hair disheveled and his fists clenched. Margaret sat stiffly in a wingback chair, her hands resting on her lap, her face pale but composed. Andrew loitered near the fireplace, attempting to light a cigarette with shaking hands, while Dr. Lang leaned against a corner table, his eyes darting nervously toward the staircase, his posture stiff. They flinched when Claire cleared her throat. “Good evening,” she began, letting her sharp gaze sweep across the room. “I suppose you all know why I’m here.” No one responded, but Victor finally stopped pacing, his dark eyes narrowing. “Well, let’s not waste time,” he said curtly. "We all know it has to be one of us.”

Claire’s eyes lingered on Victor for a moment, noting the tension in his shoulders and the suppressed anger in his voice. “I’ll start with an initial look at the scene,” she said briskly. Margaret rose from her chair. “I’ll show you,” she offered softly, her voice trembling ever so slightly. As they moved toward Evelyn’s study, Victor muttered darkly, “Might as well check her pockets while you’re at it, Margaret. I’m sure you’re dying to find whatever she left behind.” Margaret froze, her face ghostly white. Andrew, from across the room, barked a laugh. “You’re one to talk, Victor. How’s that failed business of yours these days? Still drowning in debt?” The tension was palpable, but Claire simply raised a hand to silence the bickering, her sharp eyes glinting with curiosity. “We’ll get to everyone’s alibi in due time,” she said coolly. “For now, I need clarity, not accusations.” Margaret hesitated before leading Claire down the dark hallway to the study, her heels clicking louder than necessary in the oppressive silence.

The study was as grand and imposing as the rest of the manor, with heavy burgundy curtains drawn shut and the smell of old books mingling with something faintly sour—likely the remnants of Evelyn’s poisoned drink. The lifeless body of Evelyn Blackwood still sat slumped over her massive oak desk, a delicate china teacup tipped on its side beside her outstretched hand. Claire took in the scene with a practiced, measured calm. The teacup’s rim had a faint smudge of crimson lipstick, its contents partially spilled across a pile of correspondence bearing Evelyn’s sharp, elegant handwriting. Margaret stood a few paces behind Claire, wringing her hands nervously. “I was the one who found her,” she whispered. “I came in to bring her the morning mail, as I always do, and—” Her voice broke off as she gestured helplessly toward the body. Claire knelt, inspecting the desk’s surface. Amid the spilled tea and scattered papers was something curious: a crumpled scrap of paper with hastily scrawled words. “You’ll be sorry for what you’ve done,” it read. Margaret gasped when Claire held it up. “That wasn’t here when I found her! Someone must have planted it!” Claire’s brow furrowed, but she didn’t respond, her mind already spinning with possibilities.

Claire slipped the crumpled note into an evidence bag, her eyes sharpening as a thought crept into her mind. “Who else has been in this room since you found her?” she asked, her voice calm but firm. Margaret shook her head frantically. “No one! I—I screamed when I saw her, and everyone rushed over. Victor, Andrew, Dr. Lang… they all came running. Then the police were called, and they locked the room. I swear, no one else has been here since!” Claire straightened, glancing once more at the scene. “Interesting,” she murmured, her gaze settling on the tipped teacup. She leaned in, catching the faintest whiff of bitterness mixed with the fading aroma of tea—perhaps an untraceable poison, she considered. Margaret hovered, her face pale as she watched Claire work. “Do you think it was Victor?” she blurted suddenly, her voice a mixture of fear and hesitance. “He was furious when Evelyn refused to bail him out again last week. He even said he didn’t need her money, that he’d find another way!” Claire didn’t respond immediately, her eyes narrowing as she studied Evelyn’s cold, delicate fingers. “Victor seems like he has plenty of anger,” she said carefully, “but let’s see where the evidence takes us.”

As Claire turned to leave the study, she caught a glimpse of Andrew lingering in the hallway, his back against the wall and his cigarette dangling precariously from his lips. “Can’t imagine what’s taking so long,” he said lazily, his voice laced with a hollow edge. “She’s dead, isn’t she? Don’t need a genius to figure that part out.” Claire stepped closer, studying his casual demeanor, which felt oddly rehearsed. “Death doesn’t always give us the full picture, Mr. Blackwood,” she remarked. Andrew raised an eyebrow and offered a half-smile. “Touché, detective. Still, if you ask me, I think you’ve got everything you need to know already.” His tone was light, but there was something dark simmering underneath it. Claire tilted her head, intrigued. “And what do you mean by that?” Andrew flicked the ash from his cigarette onto the marble floor. “Oh, come on. It’s no secret Aunt Evelyn had plenty of enemies. And trust me, they weren’t all outside this house.” Claire didn’t break eye contact, watching for cracks in his façade. Before she could press any further, Margaret’s hesitant voice broke the moment. “Detective?” Claire turned to find her standing awkwardly at the study door. “I think you should speak with Dr. Lang next. He… he seemed very nervous earlier. It’s not like him.” Andrew smirked as Margaret scurried away, muttering under his breath, “Everyone’s throwing each other under the bus now. Typical.”

Claire found Dr. Lang in the drawing room, sitting on the edge of an antique leather couch and fidgeting with the cuffs of his shirt. His eyes jumped up to meet hers as she entered, and for a moment, he looked like a startled animal caught in a trap. “Dr. Lang,” she greeted, her tone measured, “I need to ask you a few questions.” He nodded quickly, maybe too quickly, and motioned for her to sit, though she remained standing. “You were the family’s physician,” Claire began. “I assume you were familiar with Evelyn’s health and habits?” Dr. Lang cleared his throat. “Yes, of course,” he said, his voice strained. “Evelyn was meticulous about her health—she insisted on regular checkups, maintained a strict diet, and had no serious medical conditions that I know of. The idea that she’d…” He trailed off, his hands shaking slightly as he adjusted his glasses. Claire gave him a pointed look. “And yet, she’s dead, poisoned, according to initial findings. You’re a doctor—surely you’ve considered how that might look in your line of work.” Lang paled. “You don’t actually think I… No! I would never—I’ve devoted my entire career to healing people!” His outburst was sudden, and Claire watched him carefully. “Then perhaps you can explain,” she pressed, “why Victor mentioned seeing you carrying a small vial into the study earlier this week?” Dr. Lang’s face turned ashen, and he stumbled over his response. “That was… that was nothing! Just some herbal drops Evelyn requested for her tea to help with her insomnia. I’d never poison anyone, Detective—I swear!” But Claire noticed the slight quaver in his voice and how his hands clutched the edge of the couch as if he might fall off.

Claire let his denial hang in the air for a moment, her gaze steady and unreadable. “An interesting explanation,” she said coolly, “but let’s move on. Where were you the morning Evelyn was found?” Dr. Lang relaxed fractionally, grasping at the opportunity to clear his name. “I was in my room!” he said quickly. “I’d spent the night here—I often did when Evelyn required my oversight—and I didn’t leave until I heard Margaret’s scream.” His breath hitched, and he added nervously, “You can ask her. She remembers calling for everyone!” Claire nodded slowly but didn’t miss the way his foot tapped anxiously against the floor. “And,” she continued, “did you notice anything unusual about Evelyn’s behavior in the days leading up to her death? Any disagreements, tensions perhaps?” Dr. Lang hesitated, his eyes darting to the window as if debating whether to share more. “Well…” he began cautiously, “there was a disagreement between Evelyn and Victor the night before. Quite heated. I’d just returned from my evening check-in when I heard shouting from the study—it was unmistakably Victor’s voice. Something about being humiliated and not needing Evelyn’s interference in his affairs. But… well, Victor isn’t the type to stay calm when frustrated.” His tone softened, almost pleading. “Detective, surely you can see how volatile he can be. I may have my faults, but murder? No, that isn’t in me.” Claire simply studied him, filing away his words as the puzzle grew more tangled.

Leaving Dr. Lang to stew in his own unease, Claire returned to the grand hall where she found Victor, now seated on a bench under a towering portrait of his late aunt. He sat with his elbows on his knees, his fingers steepled against his lips as though in prayer, though his expression was anything but serene. “Victor,” Claire called out, her voice interrupting his brooding. He looked up sharply, his dark eyes narrowing as if he were bracing for a fight. “Detective,” he said curtly, straightening his posture. “Let me guess: Dr. Lang is pointing fingers at me? Typical. No subtlety in this family except for Evelyn... well, when she was alive.” He laughed bitterly, but Claire didn’t smile. “You had an argument with her last night,” she began, cutting through his attempt at sarcasm. “Witnesses heard shouting about money. You were upset, weren’t you?” Victor snorted, leaning back against the bench. “Oh, is that what this is? I’m bankrupt, therefore I must’ve killed the golden goose? Don’t waste my time, Detective. Yes, I was angry! Evelyn had a way of dangling her wealth like bait and then yanking it away whenever she got bored. But murder? Please. If I wanted to rob her blind, I wouldn’t do it by poisoning tea.” He sneered, his voice dripping with disdain. “More her style, honestly. Always enjoyed her games, didn’t she?” Claire tilted her head, ignoring his jab. “Someone left a threatening note on her desk,” she said. “Do you recognize it?” Victor stiffened briefly before recovering, his smirk tightening into a scowl. “Notes, poison, secrets—it’s almost poetic. But no, Detective, I didn’t leave her any parting words. Maybe try Andrew. He’s always been Evelyn’s golden boy. Shame he’s not as innocent as he pretends.”

Victor’s last remark lingered in Claire’s mind as she stepped into the library and found Andrew reclining in a high-backed chair, his legs stretched out and an empty whiskey glass resting loosely in one hand. The room was dimly lit, the fireplace casting flickering shadows over his sharp features. He glanced up as she approached, a lazy grin spreading across his face, though it didn’t quite reach his eyes. “Ah, Detective,” he drawled, swirling the leftover ice in the glass. “Here to interrogate me too? Or has Victor already tried to throw me under the bus?” Claire folded her arms, fixing him with a steady gaze. “Your uncle did mention your name. But I’m more interested in what you’ve been up to. People say you’ve always been Evelyn’s favorite. Funny how that can change when there’s a will involved.” Andrew laughed, sharp and hollow. “Oh, please. Don’t let them fool you with their sob stories. Being her favorite wasn’t exactly a blessing. Aunt Evelyn loved to play puppet master, pulling strings and watching us all dance. If you think I benefited from that… well, you’d be mistaken.” Claire leaned closer, her gaze piercing. “And what kind of puppet are you, Andrew? The kind that resents the strings enough to cut them?” His grin faltered for a moment, and he spoke cautiously. “She was cruel, sure, but no, I didn’t kill her. You know who you should really talk to?” He gestured toward the doorway with his glass, the ice clinking against the rim. “Margaret. Always the loyal lapdog, but then she starts acting weird lately. Don’t let the timid act fool you, Detective. People like her know more than they let on.”

Claire left Andrew lounging in his feigned nonchalance and made her way to find Margaret, who had retreated to the shadowy corner of the dining room, wringing a napkin in her trembling hands. The once-pristine white napkin was now twisted and crumpled, much like Margaret’s composure. “Margaret,” Claire began gently, pulling a chair to sit across from her. Margaret’s eyes darted up, wide and pained, like a scared rabbit caught in a trap. “I heard you had a particularly close relationship with Evelyn,” Claire said. “You knew her better than anyone. Yet, it seems some people here think you’re hiding something.” Margaret flinched, clutching the napkin tighter. “That’s ridiculous. I—Detective, I gave everything to her. I was her assistant, her confidante. She trusted me implicitly!” Her voice cracked on the last word, and Claire noticed a tear glistening in the corner of her eye. “And yet,” Claire pressed, her voice softer now but no less probing, “you’ve been acting nervous, suspicious even. Is there something you’re not telling me?” Margaret opened her mouth to respond but hesitated, as if weighing the risk of her words. Finally, she whispered, “I—I haven’t seen the note for myself, but Andrew… he’s been so jumpy lately. He and Evelyn argued a few days ago—you need to know that! She told him—” Margaret stopped abruptly, her thin lips snapping shut like a locked door. Claire raised an eyebrow. “She told him what?” Margaret’s pale hands trembled as she placed the napkin on the table like a fragile surrender. “She told him she was going to rewrite the will,” Margaret confessed shakily. “He didn’t take it well at all. He stormed out of the study after screaming that she couldn’t control him anymore.” Claire leaned back slightly, absorbing this new thread of information, watching Margaret’s frightened eyes for any sign of deception. “Curious how quick everyone is to point fingers today,” she murmured, almost to herself.

Claire stepped out of the dining room, letting Margaret’s trembling words settle in her mind like pieces of a puzzle still waiting to fit. If Evelyn had been planning to rewrite her will, it certainly added fuel to the fire. The question was, whose fire? Lost in thought, she nearly collided with Victor, who was coming up the hallway with a scowl etched deep on his face. “Finished playing good cop with Margaret?” he snapped, his sharp voice echoing off the high ceilings. Claire studied him without a word—his anger seemed genuine, but she knew better than to take surface emotions at face value. “You don’t seem to think much of her,” Claire said, probing. Victor scoffed. “Margaret? Oh, she plays the loyal servant bit well enough, but let me tell you, Detective—it’s all an act. She’s always been jealous. Spent years at Evelyn’s side like some shadow, waiting, hoping... for what? To finally be rewarded? Well, guess what—she wasn’t in the will. Not a penny.” Claire noted his certainty. “And you know this because...?” Victor smirked, shaking his head bitterly. “I overheard Aunt Evelyn talking to her lawyer last month. I was supposed to be out of the house, but, well, you’d be surprised what you overhear when you’re not meant to.” His voice turned cold. “Margaret didn’t take it well. And the day Evelyn mentioned rewriting the will? Margaret was there too. Don’t let her idiot routine fool you. She’s more dangerous than she looks.” Claire tapped her chin thoughtfully, watching Victor retreat with heavy steps. The threads of suspicion were weaving a web now, and the more they tangled, the more deliberate the misdirections felt.

As Claire made her way back to her temporary workspace near the study, she paused, her eyes narrowing as she noticed Andrew slipping quietly into Evelyn’s bedroom at the end of the hall. Intrigued, she followed silently, pressing herself along the wall outside the half-open door. Inside, Andrew stood at Evelyn’s vanity, rifling through the drawers with precise, practiced movements. He muttered under his breath, his frustration bubbling over as he slammed a drawer shut. “It has to be here,” he hissed, his voice low but urgent. Claire stepped inside, her footsteps reverberating in the stillness. “Looking for something, Andrew?” she asked, her tone sharp enough to startle him. He spun around, guilt flashing across his face before he replaced it with a forced smirk. “Just… reminiscing,” he said flippantly, gesturing to the vanity. “It’s been such a long, sentimental week, you know.” Claire’s eyes didn’t leave his. “I doubt rifling through her things will bring back warm memories,” she said. She stepped closer, her voice lowering. “What exactly were you searching for?” Andrew faltered, his cocky demeanor slipping. “Nothing important,” he muttered, his tone defensive. “Just... some letters. Aunt Evelyn loved to keep things private, and I thought—” He cut himself off, realizing he was digging himself deeper. Claire watched him carefully, her suspicions rising. “You wouldn’t, by chance, be looking for something she might have written about that will change?” she asked. For the briefest moment, Andrew’s face went pale, but he quickly masked it behind a casual shrug. “I don’t know what you’re talking about,” he said sharply, brushing past her. But as Claire watched him storm out of the room, she knew she’d just touched a nerve—and Andrew was hiding more than he let on.

The house had grown oppressively quiet as Claire caught the faint ticking of a clock somewhere in the distance. Deciding she needed clarity, she returned to the study, where Evelyn's body remained undisturbed, a ghostly reminder of the storm of motives swirling around her death. Her eyes fell back on the overturned teacup and the spilled liquid pooling across the desk, soaking into the threatening note. Pulling out her rubber gloves, she carefully inspected the edges of the note again. The handwriting was uneven, hurried, but something about it tugged at her memory. She didn’t have to wonder long. From the corner of her eye, she caught movement at the doorway. It was Margaret again, hovering nervously. “Detective, I—” Margaret stammered, stopping mid-sentence when Claire looked up sharply. “What is it?” Claire asked, her tone direct. Margaret wrung her hands together, clearly struggling with whatever she needed to say. “It’s about Victor,” she blurted finally. “He and Evelyn argued far more often than even Andrew. She—she told me she refused to fund his new project, and he was furious. He said she’d regret it. You… you have to believe me! He’s not as innocent as—” “Enough,” Claire interjected, fixing Margaret with a calm but piercing stare. “You’ve made it clear everyone in this house has a reason to hate Evelyn. But right now, your desperation to point fingers is what interests me most.” Margaret looked as though she’d been struck, her face going pale. Without another word, she turned and fled down the hall, leaving Claire standing amidst the steadily growing chaos of lies and accusations. For the first time, Claire felt she might finally see through the smokescreen.

Claire stayed in the study, her fingers brushing lightly against the desk as she replayed the accusations swirling in her mind. Then her eyes landed on the scattered correspondence once more—those letters Evelyn had been working on before her death. Among the stained envelopes and loose papers, one name kept appearing: "Andrew." Intrigued, Claire carefully picked up a partially crumpled sheet and unfolded it. The handwriting—crisp and precise, unlike the jagged scrawl on the threatening note—was unmistakably Evelyn’s. In the letter, Evelyn had written to her lawyer with unusually strong words: *“As for Andrew, his entitlement has gone far enough. I want to ensure this will reflects my intentions—he must learn, on paper or otherwise, that the world doesn’t revolve around him.”* Claire’s lips pressed into a thin line. It confirmed what Margaret had said earlier—Evelyn had intended to rewrite her will—and one thing was certain now: Andrew stood to lose as much as anyone, perhaps more. 

Just then, Claire heard the distinct, clipped sound of shoes approaching. She quickly tucked the letter into her pocket and turned to see Dr. Lang standing at the doorway. He hesitated, one hand gripping the doorframe. “Detective,” he said nervously, his face drawn and pale. “I… I’ve just remembered something that might be important.” Claire eyed him skeptically. “Oh? And what’s that?” Dr. Lang swallowed hard, his hand twitching at his side. “The vial. The one Victor told you about… It wasn’t only herbal drops.” His words stumbled over themselves. “Evelyn asked me to look into a... medication issue recently—something about avoiding accidents. I didn’t think much of it at the time, but now…” His voice dropped to a whisper. “Victor knew about it. He asked far too many questions. He was always asking about her medications. Detective, I didn’t put it together before, but... I’m starting to think he might’ve been planning this for some time.” Claire studied him carefully. His voice sounded sincere, but sincerity could easily be feigned in desperation. The web continued to tighten—and every thread seemed to lead to yet another knot of deceit.

Claire folded her arms, scrutinizing Dr. Lang as he lingered in the doorway. “That’s quite the accusation,” she said evenly. “If Victor was so interested in Evelyn’s medication, why didn’t you report it before now?” Dr. Lang lowered his gaze, shame flickering across his face. “I thought it was harmless curiosity,” he admitted. “Victor has always been nosy, always looking for an edge, but I never imagined… I should’ve seen it earlier.” Claire mulled over his words, noting the faint tremor in his voice—not betrayal, but fear. “And what about the vial?” she pressed. “Can you account for it?” Dr. Lang hesitated, licking his dry lips before responding. “It’s gone,” he admitted hoarsely. “I left it in the medicine cabinet in Evelyn’s bathroom—the last time I saw it was two days before her death. I swear, Detective, I have no reason to harm her. I—” His voice broke, and Claire raised a hand to cut him off. 

“Two days ago. Interesting,” Claire said thoughtfully. “Tell me this, Dr. Lang—did anyone else have access to Evelyn’s quarters during that time?” He paused, visibly struggling to recall, then said, “Only Margaret. She was always the one Evelyn trusted with her personal space. Not even Andrew or Victor went in there without her permission.” Claire’s brow furrowed. The picture was becoming more muddled, not clearer. Margaret had an excuse to be in Evelyn’s room—but Margaret also seemed preoccupied with deflecting suspicion onto the others. “Convenient,” Claire murmured, almost to herself, as Dr. Lang fidgeted at her silence. “Victor, Andrew, Margaret—less suspects, more tangled puppets, it seems.” The doctor’s eyes widened in alarm at her cryptic comment, but Claire ignored him, her mind already racing to connect the fractured pieces of this increasingly personal crime.

Leaving Dr. Lang to stew in his worries, Claire decided to revisit Margaret, who had since retreated to the kitchen. She found her seated near the back door, her hands wrapped tightly around a steaming cup of tea as though it might steady her nerves. Margaret looked up, startled, as Claire entered, her pale face seeming even more drawn under the harsh kitchen lighting. “I trust you’ve calmed down,” Claire remarked dryly, pulling out a chair and sitting across from her. “Dr. Lang tells me you had access to Evelyn’s medication—a vial that seems to have conveniently vanished.” Margaret froze, her cup trembling in her hands. “I… I didn’t take anything,” she stammered. “I—yes, I had access to her bathroom, but I didn’t even know about a vial!” Claire remained unfazed, her steady gaze boring into Margaret’s. “Evelyn trusted you more than anyone else in this household,” Claire pointed out. “Which makes it odd, doesn’t it, that you seem to be at the center of so many secrets?” Margaret’s teacup clattered onto its saucer as she set it down abruptly. “I didn’t kill her!” she snapped, her voice cracking. “I loved her! She was cruel at times, yes, and controlling, but I would never harm her!” Claire leaned back, watching carefully as Margaret’s frail composure teetered. “Then why are you so afraid, Margaret?” she asked quietly. “Afraid people might think the loyal assistant finally snapped?” 

Margaret shook her head violently, tears welling in her eyes. “You don’t understand,” she whispered. “She was planning to cut everyone out, not just Andrew. All of them. The last will I heard her talk about—it was supposed to leave everything to charity, every last penny! That’s why Andrew is acting so suspicious, why Victor can’t stop blaming me. They knew. They must have overheard, somehow!” Claire’s eyebrows lifted slightly, intrigued by this revelation. Another twist: none of them were to benefit from Evelyn’s fortune. If Margaret was telling the truth, it meant greed wasn’t the only motive at play—and perhaps the players were even more desperate than they appeared.

Claire let Margaret’s revelation settle in the air, like a storm cloud too heavy to disperse. “Charity,” she repeated softly, filing the detail in her mental ledger. She leaned forward, her voice firm but calm. “And when exactly did Evelyn make this decision? Was it recent?” Margaret hesitated for just a moment too long before nodding. “Y-yes,” she stammered. “About a week ago. She told me it was time to stop rewarding incompetence and selfishness—or so she put it.” Her lips twisted as if the words themselves were bitter. “She said the family didn’t deserve her money anymore. She was... so determined.” Claire studied her carefully. “And you didn’t think to mention this earlier? Surely you realize how this changes things for everyone in this house.” Margaret’s hands clenched into fists so tightly her knuckles whitened. “I didn’t think I needed to,” she said through gritted teeth. “It’s not relevant because *I* didn’t kill her! All I ever wanted was to help her, not hurt her.” 

Claire tilted her head, her mind piecing together timelines like jagged shards of glass. A week ago, Evelyn decided to rewrite her will. Two days ago, a vial disappeared. And then, Evelyn’s life abruptly ended. “Fine,” Claire said after a pause. “One last question, Margaret. Besides Andrew, did anyone else know about this new will?” Margaret’s lips parted as if to answer, but she stopped herself, the pause thick with hesitation. “I don’t know,” she finally whispered, her voice barely audible. “I didn’t tell anyone. But… Victor was around that day. He was asking questions about her meetings with the lawyer.” Claire didn’t respond, simply standing and turning toward the door. Margaret called after her, her voice tinged with desperation. “Whatever you think of me, Detective, I swear, Evelyn kept things to herself. If Victor or Andrew knew... they didn’t hear it from me.” 

Margaret’s trembling words stuck with Claire as she left. Evelyn’s decision to cut her family off had clearly thrown gasoline onto an already volatile set of relationships. But who had panicked enough to act—and why?

As Claire paced the dimly lit halls of Blackwood Manor, something tugged at her thoughts—small inconsistencies that felt like stray threads waiting to unravel. She found Victor in the smoking room, a glass of brandy perched on the edge of the table beside him, untouched. He was staring blankly out the window, his reflection fractured in the glass against the backdrop of the moonlit gardens. “Victor.” Her voice sliced through the heavy silence, and he turned, his expression guarded but weary. “Another round of questions, I assume?” he muttered, his voice flat. Claire remained standing, arms crossed. “You're awfully calm for someone who was at the center of so much conflict with Evelyn. Margaret claims you knew about the possible changes to her will. Care to explain why you didn’t mention that before?” 

Victor’s face darkened, and for a moment, guilt seemed to ripple across his features. “Because it doesn’t matter,” he said curtly. “Yes, I suspected she was going to cut me out—even joked about it the last time we fought. But if money was all I wanted, wouldn’t I have made a grander play? Poisoning tea is too...” He paused, shaking his head. “Cowardly.” He met Claire’s eyes with defiance. “Maybe you should be looking at Margaret. She’d never admit it, but she *needed* Evelyn more than anyone else here. Without Evelyn’s influence, she’s nobody.” 

Claire’s gaze didn’t waver, though she stored his words away. “Interesting perspective,” she said evenly. “But I find it curious, Victor, that despite all your insistence about not caring for Evelyn’s fortune, you had the most opportunity to overhear her plans. You were always in and out of the house, weren’t you? And didn’t Dr. Lang mention you being unusually interested in her medication?” At this, Victor’s lips pressed into a thin line, and an unmistakable flash of irritation crossed his face as he set his glass down hard. “I told you before, I didn’t poison her,” he said sharply. “If I wanted something from her, Detective, I wouldn’t have waited for her to rewrite anything. God knows there are faster ways to force someone’s hand.” The words hung in the air, heavy with implication—and maybe just a little too much honesty. As Victor glared at her, Claire’s mind teetered between his frustration and the calculated nature of the crime. The pieces weren’t quite fitting… but she felt they were close.

Claire left Victor behind, his veiled threats and simmering anger still echoing in her ears. She needed air, needed to step back from the tensions boiling over inside the house. Stepping onto the terrace, she was surprised to find Andrew, standing alone with another cigarette dangling between his fingers. He didn’t look at her as she approached, his gaze fixed on the pitch-black night beyond the estate grounds. The glowing ember in his hand pulsed faintly as he took a long drag. “Can’t sleep?” Claire asked, her tone neutral. Andrew gave a wry laugh, tipping his head slightly in her direction. “Sleep’s a luxury around here,” he said. “Imagine living your whole life in a game where every move someone makes, someone else stands ready with a knife.” 

Claire leaned against the railing beside him. “You know,” she began, her voice light but probing, “Victor seems eager to pin this all on Margaret. Margaret thinks it’s Victor. And funny enough, your name comes up just as often from both of them.” Andrew inhaled deeply, the flicker of the cigarette momentarily illuminating the dark shadows under his eyes. “Of course it does,” he replied with a smirk. “It’s easy to blame the spoiled grandson. Everyone wants me to be the villain because they can’t stomach looking at themselves.” He exhaled slowly, the smoke curling upward into the cold night air. “But the thing is, Detective, I don’t have to be the villain here. Aunt Evelyn did that job just fine herself.” 

Claire tilted her head, watching him carefully. “Yet you still tried to rifle through her belongings,” she said quietly. “Any particular reason?” Andrew finally turned to face her, his grin slipping just a little. “Look,” he said after a pause, flicking his cigarette into the garden below. “Did I hate her? Sure. Did I have something to gain from her death? Not anymore, apparently.” He gave a bitter laugh. “But I didn’t kill her, Detective. Maybe I was looking for answers. Maybe I just wanted to understand *why* she was so hell-bent on controlling all of us.” He straightened, shoving his hands into his pockets. “Whatever you’re looking for, you’re barking up the wrong tree here.” And with that, he walked off into the shadows, leaving Claire standing in the cold, the night wrapping its secrets tightly around her.

Claire remained on the terrace for a moment, letting the crisp night air cool her thoughts. Something wasn’t right—it wasn’t just the tangled motives or the shifting accusations; it was the precision of the crime itself. Evelyn Blackwood had been killed with poison, a method that required planning, subtlety, and access. It wasn’t impulsive rage. It wasn’t brute force. It was calculated. And the precision spoke of intent, of someone who had been quietly waiting for the right moment to strike. 

Turning back into the house, she caught sight of Dr. Lang pacing near the study door, his face creased with worry. “Detective,” he called nervously as she approached, shifting on his feet. “I’ve been thinking—checking Evelyn’s tea might not be enough. You should… examine her private medicines as well. She kept them in a locked drawer in the bathroom, though God knows who else has gotten into them.” His words came tumbling out, almost frantic. Claire’s brows furrowed. “That’s convenient advice,” she said coldly. “If you’re so concerned, why didn’t you mention this earlier?” 

Dr. Lang rubbed the back of his neck, stammering. “I—I didn’t think of it at first. But... what if someone tampered with them days ago? Evelyn was diligent with her dosages—I always reminded her—but if someone knew how to time it...” He broke off and looked down, visibly distressed. Claire narrowed her eyes, leaning closer. “Timing,” she repeated, her voice dangerously low. “Poisoning tea is one thing. Timing toxin exposure is another. That would require a deep understanding of her habits... or maybe even medical expertise.” 

The doctor froze in place, his face paling. “You can’t think I—” he began, but Claire cut him off sharply. “Oh, I think a lot of things, Doctor,” she said. “For now, stay exactly where you are. I’ve heard enough.” And with that, she strode past him, leaving him spluttering in her wake. Inside her head, the puzzle’s edges were beginning to take shape. Only a few pieces were still missing, but most of them were already lingering in the tangled mess of alibis, deflection, and deceit that suffocated this house.

Claire headed straight for Evelyn’s bathroom, her steps quick and deliberate. Whatever Dr. Lang was hinting at, she needed to see it for herself. From what she’d gathered, Evelyn was meticulous—if her medicines held a clue, they’d still be in the locked drawer mentioned. The polished cabinet beneath the mirror stood untouched, but her eyes landed immediately on the small, inconspicuous drawer beside the vanity. Leaning down, she tested the handle—it was indeed locked. 

Reaching for her tools, Claire worked the lock carefully, the gentle click as it opened reverberating in the silence. Inside, small, clearly labeled pill bottles lined the velvet interior. At first glance, everything appeared normal—until she noticed one bottle out of place. Its label was identical to the others, reading a generic sedative Evelyn occasionally used for sleep. However, it was unusually light, almost empty. Claire unscrewed the top and immediately noticed the faint scent—bitter, sharp, chemical. Her deduction was swift: the contents had recently been tampered with. This wasn’t an herbal drop or harmless medication; it was something far more sinister. 

She straightened, clutching the bottle as her mind raced. Dr. Lang’s earlier nervousness resurfaced in her thoughts. A doctor would certainly have the knowledge to manipulate doses, to experiment with amounts that might go unnoticed until the fatal moment—but was it too obvious? Then, she remembered: Margaret had access to the room too. And Victor. And Andrew. But who had the combination of motive, opportunity, and cold calculation to do this? The answer was narrowing, sharpening in her mind as the pieces began falling into place. Claire knew one thing for certain now—this bottle was the key to unraveling it all.

Claire returned the bottle to the drawer carefully, her mind buzzing with the implications. By the time she emerged from Evelyn's bathroom, the tension in the manor was suffocating. She needed answers, and she needed them now. As she made her way back toward the main hall, she stopped short at the sight of Margaret and Andrew locked in a heated argument near the library. Margaret looked frantic, clutching her apron with trembling hands, while Andrew loomed over her, his face dark with anger. 

“You’re lying!” Andrew hissed, his voice low but venomous. “Don’t think I don’t know what you’ve been doing, slinking around like that.” 

Margaret stumbled back, her voice desperate. “I’ve done nothing but serve this family! You’re the one who’s been sneaking into rooms and tearing things apart. What were you looking for in Evelyn’s things, Andrew? What are you hiding?” 

Claire stepped forward, her voice cutting through the tension like a knife. “Enough.” Both Margaret and Andrew froze, turning toward her with guilty expressions. “You two seem to be accusing each other of quite a lot,” Claire said, her tone sharp. “But while you’ve been busy squabbling, I’ve uncovered something that changes everything.” 

Andrew crossed his arms but didn’t speak, while Margaret’s lips quivered. “What did you find?” she asked shakily. 

Claire studied them both for a long moment. “Evelyn’s sedatives. One bottle has been tampered with, and I’d wager the poison was introduced in just the right doses to mimic a natural decline. Slow, gradual—until the final dose in her tea.” She stepped closer, her gaze boring into them. “Now, unless one of you wants me to assume the worst, I suggest you tell me the truth about what you’ve been hiding. All of it.” 

Margaret visibly paled, but it was Andrew who broke first, his face twisting with fury. “And what about Victor?” he snapped. “Have you asked him why he was so interested in her things? Or why he knew Evelyn’s schedule down to the minute?” His anger seemed explosive, but Claire couldn’t miss the edge of panic creeping into his voice. The loose threads were tightening, and she was almost ready to pull.

The storm of accusations crashing around her only made Claire’s focus clearer. She ignored Andrew’s outburst and turned her fiery gaze to Margaret, who now clutched the edge of a nearby table for balance. “Margaret,” Claire said coldly, stepping closer. “You’ve been quick to play the frightened witness, but you’ve known more about everyone’s motives than you should. You knew about Evelyn’s decision to rewrite her will. You knew about Andrew’s anger, Victor’s desperation, even the things Evelyn kept locked away. You’ve worked for her for years—in her shadow—but now, when everything is crumbling, you’re emerging with carefully timed accusations. Why is that?” 

Margaret’s face crumpled, her lip trembling like a child caught in a lie. “I—I never meant—!” she began, but Claire held up a hand, cutting her off. “You told me Evelyn trusted you implicitly, yet her death was carried out in a way that required the kind of knowledge only someone close to her could have. The tampered sedatives? The bitter tea? They weren’t a blunt act of rage but a slow, deliberate murder. One planned by someone who wanted this house pulled apart piece by piece after Evelyn’s death.” Claire’s voice grew sharper. “And that someone is you, isn’t it?”

Margaret sagged against the table, her frantic breathing filling the silence as both Andrew and Victor—who had stepped into the room unnoticed—stared in stunned disbelief. “No! You don’t understand!” Margaret finally cried out. “I didn’t want her dead! I just—she was cruel, controlling, always looking down on me after everything I sacrificed for her. This family didn’t deserve her money, but neither did SHE! I only wanted her to feel small, powerless, even for a moment. I didn’t mean for her to die...” Her voice broke, tears streaming down her face as she folded into herself. 

“It was you,” Claire said coolly, circling her like a predator around wounded prey. “You administered small doses of poison through the sedatives, knowing Evelyn trusted you without question. You kept suspicion off yourself—I’ll admit, you played your role well. But the note on her desk? ‘You’ll be sorry for what you’ve done.’ That slip of anger—it gave you away.” Margaret’s sobs turned to gasping breaths as the weight of her crime bore down on her. The room was silent but for the thick sound of her sorrow. Claire straightened, her gaze moving toward Victor and Andrew. “I suggest you both stop bickering. The truth always finds its way through, even tangled in a web of lies.”

The morning broke cold and gray as Margaret was escorted out of Blackwood Manor in trembling silence by the local authorities. The remaining occupants—Victor, Andrew, and Dr. Lang—stood in uneasy quiet as Claire gathered her things, their faces pale from the night’s revelations. The house, stripped of its secrets, seemed larger now, emptier, and filled with nothing but the echoes of Evelyn’s shadow. 

Victor leaned against the doorway, his arms crossed tightly over his chest. “I never would’ve thought it was her,” he muttered, his voice hollow. “Margaret... pathetic little Margaret.” Andrew shot him a pointed look but said nothing, his gaze fixed on the ground. Dr. Lang finally spoke, his voice soft and tinged with guilt. “She fooled all of us. Played into her own act of devotion. Maybe we were too busy blaming each other to see it.” 

But Claire, buttoning up her trench coat, turned toward them with a sharp, knowing gaze. “She might’ve carried it through, but don’t make the mistake of thinking you’re unrelated to her motives,” she said coldly. “Evelyn didn’t just poison herself with sedatives—she poisoned this family, one cruel game at a time. Margaret was merely her final move, a pawn turned queen, acting in a moment of desperation. And all of you? Well, you were the pieces Evelyn spent years playing with, until someone finally tipped the board over.”

Victor clenched his jaw, but he stayed silent as Claire picked up her suitcase and headed toward the front door. Before stepping out into the gray light of dawn, she turned back once more. "In the end, every one of you had a motive, and your hands aren't as clean as you think. But justice rarely cares for complexities—it cares for facts. And the fact is, Evelyn Blackwood built a house of cards that someone was bound to blow over eventually." With that, she stepped out into the morning, leaving the broken family behind, trapped in the web their matriarch had spun long before her final cup of tea.

Before Claire could probe further, heavy footsteps announced Victor’s arrival in the drawing room. “Herbal drops, huh?” Victor sneered, leaning against the doorway with a dark, sardonic grin. “Interesting choice of words, Doc. Especially when you’ve been walking around this house like a guilt-ridden ghost ever since yesterday.” Dr. Lang shot to his feet, his face flushed. “That’s enough, Victor!” he snapped, his usually measured tone breaking into anger. “Just because you’ve made yourself the family’s resident failure doesn’t mean you can throw baseless accusations around!” Victor laughed coldly, his arms crossed. “Oh, trust me, I don’t need to throw anything. Everyone knows you were the last person to see Evelyn alone before she turned up dead.” Claire’s brow furrowed at this revelation, and she turned to Lang. “Is that true?” she asked sharply. The doctor hesitated, his jaw tightening. “I spoke with Evelyn in the study the evening before her death,” he admitted, reluctantly meeting her gaze. “She asked me for advice on calming her nerves—she’d been under a lot of stress lately. I left her perfectly fine and alive.” But Victor pressed on, his voice dripping with venom. “Stress? Or guilt? Maybe it’s easier to sleep at night after you’ve silenced the one person who knew something you didn’t want getting out.” Dr. Lang opened his mouth to retort, but his face twisted as if the words were caught in his throat. Claire stood silently, observing the dynamic between them—and the cracks starting to widen.

Claire let his denial hang in the air for a moment, her gaze steady and unreadable. “An interesting explanation,” she said coolly, “but let’s move on. Where were you the morning Evelyn was found?” Dr. Lang relaxed fractionally, grasping at the opportunity to clear his name. “I was in my room!” he said quickly. “I’d spent the night here—I often did when Evelyn required my oversight—and I didn’t leave until I heard Margaret’s scream.” His breath hitched, and he added nervously, “You can ask her. She remembers calling for everyone!” Claire nodded slowly but didn’t miss the way his foot tapped anxiously against the floor. “And,” she continued, “did you notice anything unusual about Evelyn’s behavior in the days leading up to her death? Any disagreements, tensions perhaps?” Dr. Lang hesitated, his eyes darting to the window as if debating whether to share more. “Well…” he began cautiously, “there was a disagreement between Evelyn and Victor the night before. Quite heated. I’d just returned from my evening check-in when I heard shouting from the study—it was unmistakably Victor’s voice. Something about being humiliated and not needing Evelyn’s interference in his affairs. But… well, Victor isn’t the type to stay calm when frustrated.” His tone softened, almost pleading. “Detective, surely you can see how volatile he can be. I may have my faults, but murder? No, that isn’t in me.” Claire simply studied him, filing away his words as the puzzle grew more tangled.

Claire strode into the parlor where Andrew now lounged on a chaise, swirling a glass of brandy with an air of nonchalance that was almost theatrical. “Detective,” he said, his tone syrupy sweet, “I trust the wolves are already at each other’s throats? Uncle Victor’s temper, Margaret’s paranoia, Dr. Lang’s shaking hands… You must love a room full of suspects.” Claire ignored the bait and cut straight to the point. “Victor implied you might have something to hide, Andrew. Care to enlighten me before I uncover it myself?” Andrew’s grin faltered just enough for her to notice. He took a slow sip of his drink before answering. “Victor’s always hated me. Big surprise he’d point fingers.” He set the glass down with a deliberate clink and leaned forward, resting his elbows on his knees. “What exactly do you think I’ve done, Detective? I’m very curious.” Claire didn’t miss the sharp edge of challenge in his voice. “You tell me,” she replied evenly. “You were close to Evelyn, weren’t you? She favored you over the others. But favorites have their own kind of pressure, don’t they? Maybe she turned that favor against you when you didn’t toe the line.” Andrew’s smile vanished entirely, replaced by something cold, almost calculating. “If you’re suggesting I killed her to get out from under her thumb, you’re barking up the wrong tree,” he said, his voice low. “I didn’t need to. Evelyn trusted me more than anyone. She was practically grooming me to take over everything. Why would I kill my best chance at inheriting the entire estate?” He leaned back, though his jaw tightened slightly. “No, Detective. If someone killed Evelyn, it’s because they’d already lost her favor—and her money. But as for me? I had nothing to lose.”

Claire found Andrew in the parlor, nursing a glass of whiskey despite the early hour. The fire crackled behind him, casting flickering shadows across his face as he reclined lazily in a high-backed chair. He glanced up when Claire entered, his blue eyes gleaming with a mix of arrogance and defiance. “Ah, the esteemed detective returns,” he drawled, swirling the amber liquid in his glass. “What’s the verdict? Decided which of us gets the noose yet?” Claire ignored his taunt, stepping closer with her hands in her coat pockets. “My verdict depends on facts, not wit,” she replied crisply. “Speaking of, let’s talk about the morning of Evelyn’s death. Where were you?” Andrew smirked as if the question amused him. “Where I always am at that ungodly hour—sleeping. You can ask the staff. They know I don’t emerge before noon.” Claire raised an eyebrow. “Convenient. But what about last night? What were you and Evelyn discussing in the study before the argument started?” The smirk on his face faltered just slightly, a crack in his polished demeanor. “I stopped by to say goodnight,” he said smoothly. “We exchanged some words, but nothing serious. She was upset about some business dealings I’d made without consulting her—she nagged, I laughed, the usual cat-and-mouse routine. Hardly a motive for murder, don’t you think?” Claire leaned forward. “Upset enough to threaten cutting you out of the will? Margaret hinted Evelyn had been revising documents in the study.” Andrew set his glass down harder than necessary, his mask of nonchalance flickering. “Don’t be ridiculous. I know how to stay in Evelyn’s good graces when it matters. Unlike others in this house, I didn’t need to grovel for her attention—or her money.” But as Claire stepped back, she couldn’t help but notice his fingers twitching beside his now-empty glass, and a faint bead of sweat at his temple.

Claire found Andrew in the garden, pacing along the gravel path beneath the bare branches of a withered oak tree. He looked up as she approached, his usual smirk replaced by a nervous grimace. The remnants of his cigarette smoldered between his fingers, even though he barely seemed to notice it. “Do I get my turn now?” he asked with mock cheerfulness, though his voice lacked conviction. Claire regarded him calmly. “Let’s talk about your relationship with your grandmother,” she said. “Victor seems to think you were her favorite.” Andrew barked a short laugh, tossing his cigarette to the ground and crushing it underfoot. “Favorite? Sure, if you can call being her puppet a compliment. Evelyn liked control—always pulling strings, trying to mold me into her little legacy. It wasn’t love; it was obligation.” He shoved his hands into his coat pockets and looked away, his jaw tightening. “But I played along. I played my part.” “Interesting,” Claire said, watching his every twitch. “Were you playing along when you argued with her three days ago? Witnesses say they overheard shouting near the conservatory.” Andrew’s head snapped back toward her, his eyes wide for a fraction of a second before narrowing. “Who told you that? Margaret?” He snorted and shook his head. “It wasn’t even an argument—it was just… a misunderstanding. Grandma…” He trailed off, his face darkening. “Let’s just say she had a talent for pushing buttons. But I didn’t kill her, if that’s what you’re fishing for, Detective. I don’t have the stomach for it. Maybe Victor does, though. Or Margaret. She’d do anything for this family… anything.” The way he said it was loaded with an edge of malice, and Claire made a note of it. “Where were you this morning, Andrew?” she pressed. He hesitated, his mouth twitching. “In my room, asleep. Like everyone else. What do you want me to say?” His answer sounded practiced, and Claire filed it away with the rest of his contradictions.

Claire found Andrew in the solarium, the afternoon light spilling through the glass walls to catch the faint sheen of sweat on his brow. He had traded his cigarette for a glass of whiskey, the amber liquid swirling lazily in his hand as he leaned against a marble pillar. “You look deep in thought,” Claire said as she approached, and Andrew glanced up, flashing her an easy, almost disarming grin. “Detective, you caught me,” he drawled, raising the glass in an ironic salute. “Just contemplating the tragedy of it all. Aunt Evelyn taken so cruelly—what kind of monster could do such a thing?” There was a faint mockery in his tone, as if he were enjoying the game more than he should. “Good question,” Claire replied, fixing her gaze on him. “That kind of monster might be closer than you think. When exactly did you last see your aunt alive?” Andrew shrugged, taking a sip of his drink. “Last night, just before dinner. She was muttering about some papers she needed Margaret to review. I didn’t stick around—Evelyn liked to lecture, and I wasn’t in the mood for one of her sermons.” He smirked briefly, but Claire didn’t miss the tension in the way he gripped the glass. “Did she seem upset, agitated?” she pressed. Andrew hesitated just long enough for it to register. “She seemed fine. Tired, maybe. Though if anyone upset her, it was probably Victor. Or Margaret. Oh, or Dr. Lang. Pick your poison, Detective. Evelyn had a way of making people either adore her or resent her.” His words were light, but his eyes betrayed something sharper—a guardedness that made Claire wonder what exactly he wasn’t saying.

Claire found Andrew lounging on the veranda, a glass of brandy cradled in his hand as he gazed out over the fog-covered grounds. The distant howl of a wolf punctuated the stillness, and he didn’t turn when Claire approached. “Lovely family reunion, isn’t it?” he remarked without looking back, his tone dripping with sarcasm. Claire stepped closer, crossing her arms. “Victor seems eager to place you at the center of this mess,” she said. Andrew chuckled dryly and finally turned to face her, his demeanor as smug as ever. “Victor’s always got something to say, doesn’t he?” He gestured for her to sit, but she remained standing, her eyes fixed on his. “You were close to Evelyn, weren’t you?” she pressed. “Victor claims you were her favorite, the ‘golden boy.’” Andrew smirked but there was a flicker of something darker beneath the surface. “Sure, she had a soft spot for me. I didn’t need her money, though, if that’s what you’re driving at. But if you’re asking whether I had a reason to kill her—leave me out of that circus. I’ve got a clean conscience, Detective.” He stood now, towering over Claire, and added quietly, “But maybe you should ask Margaret. Victor’s last remark lingered in Claire’s mind as she stepped into the library and found Andrew reclining in a high-backed chair, his legs stretched out and an empty whiskey glass resting loosely in one hand. The room was dimly lit, the fireplace casting flickering shadows over his sharp features. He glanced up as she approached, a lazy grin spreading across his face, though it didn’t quite reach his eyes. “Ah, Detective,” he drawled, swirling the leftover ice in the glass. “Here to interrogate me too? The kind that resents the strings enough to cut them?” His grin faltered for a moment, and he spoke cautiously. “She was cruel, sure, but no, I didn’t kill her. You know who you should really talk to?” He gestured toward the doorway with his glass, the ice clinking against the rim. “Margaret. Always the loyal lapdog, but then she starts acting weird lately. Claire sat in silence for a moment, letting Margaret’s trembling confession settle as the clock in the dining room ticked steadily like a heartbeat. Finally, she stood, her heels echoing faintly on the polished wood floor. “Thank you, Margaret,” she said, her tone unreadable. “I’ll keep that in mind.” Margaret nodded miserably, dabbing her damp eyes with the crumpled napkin, clearly relieved that the questions were over—at least for now.  

Claire returned to the study to examine the note again, pulling it from the evidence bag with gloved hands. The handwriting was jagged, rushed, but curiously neat in its own way. Just then, Claire leaned closer to the desk, her sharp eyes catching something she’d missed earlier: faint indentations pressed into the blotter pad beneath Evelyn’s correspondence. Claire left Margaret to her trembling confession, her mind swirling with the growing web of accusations and motives. Margaret’s revelation lingered in Claire’s mind as she strolled back into the foyer. The dramatic ripples caused by the mere mention of the will were impossible to ignore. Andrew, with his cavalier charm, suddenly seemed more volatile. Yet, Victor’s simmering rage and Margaret’s own timid unease were just as telling. Alone.” Claire studied him, noting the beads of sweat forming on his brow despite the coolness of the manor. “What is it, Doctor?” she asked, her voice carefully neutral. Lang glanced toward the dark hallway leading to the study, then back at Claire. “I’ve been trying to tell you… something’s not right about the timeline.” He hesitated, his hands gripping the banister tightly. “Victor wasn’t the last one in the study that night. Claire stepped away to gather her thoughts, the pieces of the puzzle swirling in her mind like a chaotic storm. Each suspect painted a damning picture of someone else, yet none of them quite fit together. As she paced back toward the foyer, her eyes fell on a small, locked cabinet tucked beneath the grand staircase, its presence easy to overlook in the grandeur of the manor. Something about it struck her—a faint smear near the polished brass handle, dark and out of place. Kneeling, she examined it closer and realized it was a smudge of dried tea—or was it something else? Claire called for the housekeeper, Mrs. Audley, an elderly woman with keen eyes who’d worked at Blackwood Manor for decades. “Who has access to this cabinet?” Claire asked, gesturing to the small lock. Mrs. Audley hesitated. “Only Miss Evelyn kept the keys, Detective,” the woman wheezed. “She didn’t like anyone tampering with her valuables.” “Valuables?” Claire asked, her curiosity piqued. Mrs. Audley nodded reluctantly. “She used to keep private things there—her documents, letters… and a few vials Dr. Lang prepared, special remedies for her tea.” Claire’s stomach tightened. “You’re saying Dr. Lang’s herbal drops are in this cabinet?” Mrs. Audley shrugged helplessly. “I wouldn’t know for sure. I only clean around it. But I know Miss Evelyn trusted him with her concoctions.” The faint tea stain on the lock burned in Claire’s mind as a nagging suspicion began to take root. Something was being hidden—and, as always, someone had the key.

The revelation about the will added more weight to Andrew’s already suspicious behavior, and Claire decided it was time to examine Evelyn’s personal papers. Returning to the study, she sifted carefully through the pile of correspondence strewn across the desk. Invitations, business dealings, scrawled notes from acquaintances—all mundane enough—until she found an envelope marked “CONFIDENTIAL” in Evelyn’s sharp handwriting. Inside was a partially completed draft of what appeared to be a new will. Claire’s eyes lingered on Andrew’s name, clearly written in Evelyn’s hand, with a single line slashing through it, as though it had been angrily struck out. Beneath it sat Margaret’s name, underlined twice, with a note in the margin: “For her loyalty.” Claire frowned and set the paper down thoughtfully. 

Margaret had conveniently left out this detail, clearly aware of its implications—being named a beneficiary would give her the strongest motive of all. Yet Margaret’s pale face and nervous hands hardly seemed the composure of a killer. Then there was Andrew’s reaction. Did Evelyn’s intentions, even if unfulfilled, sow a vengeful seed in her nephew? Or, worse, had Margaret forged this amendment to throw suspicion elsewhere? Claire’s keen eye shifted to the threatening note still sealed in the evidence bag. The handwriting didn’t match Evelyn’s—it was jagged and hurried, inconsistent with the elegance of the will draft. Someone else’s hand had brought that note to light. Unanswerable questions swirled as Claire realized the web of suspicion stretched further than she initially thought.

Claire stepped out of the dining room, letting Margaret’s trembling words settle in her mind like pieces of a puzzle still waiting to fit. If Evelyn had been planning to rewrite her will, it certainly added fuel to the fire. The question was, whose fire? Lost in thought, she nearly collided with Victor, who was coming up the hallway with a scowl etched deep on his face. “Finished playing good cop with Margaret?” he snapped, his sharp voice echoing off the high ceilings. Claire studied him without a word—his anger seemed genuine, but she knew better than to take surface emotions at face value. “You don’t seem to think much of her,” Claire said, probing. Victor scoffed. “Margaret? Oh, she plays the loyal servant bit well enough, but let me tell you, Detective—it’s all an act. She’s always been jealous. Spent years at Evelyn’s side like some shadow, waiting, hoping... for what? To finally be rewarded? Well, guess what—she wasn’t in the will. Not a penny.” Claire noted his certainty. “And you know this because...?” Victor smirked, shaking his head bitterly. “I overheard Aunt Evelyn talking to her lawyer last month. I was supposed to be out of the house, but, well, you’d be surprised what you overhear when you’re not meant to.” His voice turned cold. “Margaret didn’t take it well. And the day Evelyn mentioned rewriting the will? Margaret was there too. Don’t let her idiot routine fool you. She’s more dangerous than she looks.” Claire tapped her chin thoughtfully, watching Victor retreat with heavy steps. The threads of suspicion were weaving a web now, and the more they tangled, the more deliberate the misdirections felt.

Claire lingered in Evelyn’s bedroom after Andrew’s hasty exit, her eyes scanning the room with the meticulous attention of someone who knew secrets had a way of leaving traces. Evelyn seemed like the sort who would have kept her most sensitive materials somewhere private but accessible. “Someone didn’t get this far,” Claire murmured to herself, rising and glancing around the room. That’s when something odd caught her eye: a small porcelain trinket box on the bedside table, painted with delicate roses. "Too easy," she thought as she knelt again and turned the key in the lock of the vanity drawer. The drawer slid open with barely a sound, revealing a stack of papers bound together with a silk ribbon. Claire’s heart quickened as she fingered through the documents: neatly typed correspondence, some letters written in Evelyn’s sharp handwriting, and, finally, a folded draft of what could only be a new will. “So, it wasn’t just talk,” Claire muttered, her pulse steady as she deciphered the name of the primary beneficiary: “Margaret Holloway.” Claire frowned, her mind tripping over the implications. Margaret, who had claimed loyalty and poverty, whose hands never stopped shaking—it didn’t match the behavior of someone poised to inherit a fortune. Unless, of course, she hadn’t known. Or… unless she’d panicked that Evelyn would change her mind one last time. Detectives didn’t believe in coincidences, and this story was building toward something darker.

Claire lingered in Evelyn’s bedroom, her keen eyes scanning the space Andrew had just ransacked. The vanity drawer he’d slammed caught her attention. She pulled it open to find a disarray of papers—receipts, empty stationery envelopes, and old family photos—but tucked near the back was something curious. A yellowed envelope with Evelyn’s firm handwriting scrawled across it: “For Margaret – Confidential.” Claire carefully slid the envelope into her pocket for later examination, just as a faint sound drew her attention nearby—a soft creak. Turning sharply toward the source, she found Dr. Lang standing just inside the doorframe, his fingers gripping the edge of the door as though unsure whether to commit to entering. 

“Detective, my apologies,” he said, his voice strained as usual, “but you shouldn’t be wandering about alone in here.” Claire raised an eyebrow. “And you?” she countered, setting the drawer shut again. “Is there a medical reason you’re hovering around the victim’s bedroom?” Dr. Lang hesitated, his eyes dancing nervously to the room’s contents. “I-I just... I wanted to see if anyone needed me. This entire ordeal is unraveling everyone, and it’s... my duty to ensure—” He stopped as her stony silence made it clear his excuse was unconvincing. He shifted awkwardly, then added, “Andrew. He’s not... well. He’s agitated. You’ve surely noticed.” 

Claire studied him, unimpressed by his deflection. “Dr. Lang,” she said pointedly, “if the walls of this house could talk, whose secrets do you suppose they’d reveal first? Yours?” The doctor flinched but quickly composed himself, offering a stiff, nervous smile. “I’ve done nothing wrong, Detective,” he said, his voice faltering just enough to betray his discomfort. “But mark my words—there’s more chaos coming. And perhaps,” he added with a hesitant glance at the vanity, “you’re looking in the wrong place.” Then, just as quickly as he appeared, he turned and retreated, leaving Claire to wonder if his nervousness was guilt—or just fear of what she might find.

Claire lingered in Evelyn’s bedroom after Andrew’s abrupt departure, taking a moment to survey the space he’d been so frantically searching. The room was tastefully austere, with only a few personal touches—a delicate porcelain jewelry box, a framed family photo on the nightstand, and a stack of books neatly arranged on a shelf. But the vanity where Andrew had been rummaging caught her attention. As she opened the drawers, it became clear he hadn’t been searching at random. Several compartments had been pulled apart, leaving their contents spilled and disorganized. Amid the mess, Claire found a small leather-bound journal tucked in the back of one drawer, its calfskin cover worn from years of use.

Most of the text detailed her day-to-day affairs—meetings with lawyers, household concerns, and observations on her family. Andrew is no better. His charm won’t fool me any longer. I’ve decided it’s time to make the necessary changes. Margaret, of course, doesn’t know. I wouldn’t dare tell her yet. The words hit Claire like a sudden chill. The entry was cryptic but damning for all four suspects, layering the intrigue even further. Carefully, Claire slipped the journal into her bag, her resolve hardening. Evelyn had clearly anticipated a storm brewing around her, but someone had acted before she could take control.

Claire lingered in Evelyn’s bedroom, her eyes trailing over the vanity that Andrew had been so frantically searching. The drawers had been left ajar, their contents slightly askew—carefully folded handkerchiefs, a delicate pearl necklace, and an assortment of correspondence that appeared untouched. But as Claire’s fingers brushed the surface of the vanity, she noticed a faint smudge of ink on the wood near one drawer. Frowning, she opened it again, this time pulling everything out with precision. Beneath a stack of stationery, she found a folded piece of paper that looked out of place—rough around the edges, as if torn hurriedly. Was this proof of Evelyn’s intention to disinherit someone, or to cut someone out entirely? And more importantly, had Andrew gotten wind of it? Claire folded the letter gently and slipped it into her notebook for safekeeping. Just as she did, the bedroom door creaked open. Margaret stood in the doorway, her face pale as a ghost. “Detective,” she stammered, her eyes darting nervously to the vanity. “What… what are you doing in here?” Claire didn’t respond immediately, her gaze honing in on Margaret. “Funny,” she said evenly. “I was about to ask you the same thing.” Margaret’s hands fluttered in front of her as though trying to conjure an excuse. “I just… I thought I saw Andrew come in here. I wanted to make sure he wasn’t…” Her voice faltered, and Claire’s stare only deepened. “We should talk about what you’re so afraid I might find,” Claire said coldly, her tone making Margaret visibly shrink.

Claire lingered in Evelyn’s bedroom, her eyes scanning the opulent space for any clues Andrew might have been after. The vanity was meticulous for someone who had supposedly been rifling through it; Andrew had been careful to mask his intrusion, leaving no drawer ajar or item disturbingly misplaced. But just as Claire was about to give up, something caught her eye—a key, small and tarnished, taped beneath the bottom drawer of the vanity. Curious, she carefully removed it and examined it in the faint glow of the bedside lamp. Before she could think further about the key, her focus shifted to a faint rustling sound behind her. She turned sharply to find Margaret standing in the doorway, her pale face drawn in tight lines of worry. “Detective,” she said, wringing her hands again, “what are you doing in here? This room—it’s like a shrine—no one comes in here…” She trailed off, staring at the vanity as though willing herself not to crumble. Claire raised a brow, her voice calm but inquisitive. “Strange. Andrew seemed awfully keen on this shrine just moments ago.” Margaret straightened abruptly, color flushing into her cheeks. “Andrew? In here? What was he doing?” she rasped, her voice thin and strained. Not answering immediately, Claire instead studied the woman. “He said something about letters,” Claire replied, watching Margaret’s expression carefully.
